newsitem.title: UK: Yen soft in late Europe after mild G7 meeting.
newsitem.headline: Yen soft in late Europe after mild G7 meeting.

text.p: The yen weakened against the dollar and mark by late European trade, sold off after the G7 meeting over the weekend turned out to be more benign about the US-Japan trade gap than the market had expected.

"Dollar/yen has been strong and buying in mark/yen has been very active indeed...it's been that way since people realised that the US-Japan trade issue had not really been in the limelight at the G7," said one trader at a Japanese bank here.
"The theme today has been whether dollar/yen can keep its gains and establish a foothold above 115. But getting to 116 yen is looking difficult," he said.
The dollar was quoted at 115.24/34 yen at 1540 GMT, off its session high at 115.67 but well above its late Friday European levels of 114.51/56.
Mark/yen rose to 67.10, its highest in two weeks, although it later subsided to 66.96/99 compared to Friday's 66.25/27.

At the Denver summit, U.S. President Bill Clinton warned that if Japan's trade surplus with Washington continues to grow, there was a risk of an economic war between the two nations. Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto, for his part, said the recent burgeoning in the contentious surplus was due to temporary factors and unlikely to last for long.

Analysts said that now the G7 meeting was over -- and turned out to be something of a non-event as far as the markets were concerned -- the market would now turn its attention to the Bank of Japan's quarterly "tankan", a closely watched survey of corporate sentiment, which is due out late on Tuesday.
The tankan's key diffusion index for manufacturers for the second quarter of 1997 is forecast to show a decline of 0.8 after a rise of 2.0 previously.
"The market's anticipating a weak tankan, but that expectation is very very much priced into the market," said Sonja Gibbs, market strategist at Nomura International here.

"It would have to be very weak indeed to get the dollar to go higher," Gibbs said, adding that the risk was rather to the dollar/yen's downside should the tankan turn out to be stronger than anticipated.
Dollar/mark received no lasting support from the G7 although it got a boost in early trade in line with dollar/yen. It was at 1.7202/12 marks against 1.7295/00 in late Europe on Friday.
Analysts said it was difficult for the dollar to gain as strongly against the mark because of recent economic indicators showing the German economy was regaining its health.

"In terms of dollar/mark, the tendency of the German data in the past couple of weeks has been suggesting a slightly stronger economy. People are starting to stop writing off the German economy," Nomura's Gibbs said.

Data released on Monday showed German producer prices for May rose 0.2 percent month-on-month and 1.1 percent on the year, broadly in line with forecasts. Consumer prices in the German state of Bavaria rose 0.2 percent on the month in June and 1.6 pct year-on-year, also in line with expectations.
Analysts added, however, that although the numbers were good, data were not the key factor for moves in the mark now.

"The market doesn't react to data out of Germany in a strong way, rather, it is concerned about European monetary union and its stability," said Elizabeth Legge, senior economist at Bankgesellschaft Berlin.

In other currencies, sterling rose on heightened perceptions of higher interest rates in Britain. It hit a 59-month high of 2.8700 marks and a five-month peak of $1.6706 against its late Friday levels of 2.8605/15 and $1.6548/53.
On the European crosses, the lira rose to a four-month high of 976.60 to the mark on perceptions that Italy would join EMU in 1999. Mark/lira ended at 977.85/10 on Friday.
